value: A capability some cloud access security brokers use to detect anomalies in users' cloud access behaviour, as SP 800-215 describes it.
reason: The source mentions UEBA only as a CASB feature that detects anomalies in users' cloud access; the old back generalised it to any behaviour and made UEBA itself stop attacks.

value: SP 800-215 lists it under brokers' tracking of threats such as account hijacking, and says this can help stop insider threats and advanced attacks. It gives no wider definition.
reason: Keeps the thin primer to what SP 800-215 p. 17 says.

value: How does SP 800-209 apply need to know to access rights on storage systems?
reason: SP 800-209 does not define need to know; it uses it as the basis for assigning storage access rights.

value: Each access right, such as read, write, execute, modify or delete, should be assigned individually, based on need-to-know requirements.
reason: The old back presented the assignment rule as a definition and added "only", which the source does not say.

value: Rights are granted one by one because a person needs them for their work, not as a bundle. SP 800-53 also treats a change in someone's need to know as a trigger for telling account managers.
reason: Explains why, and links to the AC-2 card instead of implying SP 800-209 defines the term.

value: Emergency patching installs an available patch in a crisis; emergency mitigation temporarily reduces the risk before any patch exists.
reason: The old back described only one side of the contrast; SP 800-40 p. 19 gives both.

value: What are three factors, among others, that SP 800-53 says organisations consider when entering into alternate telecommunications agreements?
reason: The source says "factors such as", so the list is not closed.

value: Like comparing backup broadband providers on whether they can serve you, how good their service is, and whether you can get to it.
reason: The old example defined quality of service as speed and steadiness, which CP-8 does not say.

value: The extent of the disruption, any damage, and the expected recovery time.
reason: "In effect, a damage assessment" was the card's own inference placed in the back as if from SP 800-34.

value: SP 800-34 calls this step an outage assessment; this deck treats it as the damage assessment the exam names. Its results help the contingency plan coordinator run the recovery.
reason: Marks the link to the exam term as the deck's, not the source's.

value: SP 800-34 says disk redundancy can be provided by implementing RAID, and lists RAID among technologies to consider for a recovery strategy.
reason: "The way" overstated "can be provided"; section 3.4.1 (PDF p. 34) also lists RAID.

value: Any two of: commercial contracts with alternate site vendors, reciprocal agreements with internal or external organisations, service-level agreements with equipment vendors.
reason: The source says "internal or external organizations"; "other organisations" dropped the internal case.

value: SP 800-215 spells out CD as continuous deployment, while SP 800-190 speaks of continuous delivery. SP 800-215 treats the pipelines as building blocks of DevSecOps.
reason: The cited passage expands CI/CD as "continuous integration/continuous deployment", not delivery as the front says.

value: What are two forms of risk modelling the SSDF suggests for assessing a software design's security risk?
reason: The front asked for all forms but the back accepts any two.

value: Both CWE names describe input that is not neutralised; what differs is where it ends up, a database command or a web page.
reason: The names also differ in wording ("special elements" against "input"), so "differ only in" was inaccurate.

value: A widely agreed ranking of the most critical security risks to web applications, which OWASP publishes to make developers aware of them.
reason: Tier C (CONTENT-POLICY.md §3): the old back followed the home page's sentences closely; this keeps the facts in our own words.

value: In OWASP's account, the usual result is that people see, alter or wipe data they should not reach, or do things their role does not allow.
reason: Tier C: the old explanation tracked OWASP's sentence clause by clause.

value: A flaw where data a user supplies is passed to an interpreter, which then carries out some of that data as instructions.
reason: Tier C: the old back reused OWASP's definition almost word for word.

value: It covers what NIST calls data poisoning, and model poisoning as well.
reason: The OWASP entry is "Data and Model Poisoning", so it is broader than NIST's data poisoning alone.
